narration: Born of a Royal Insult: The Secret Stem of Kathakali

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Ramanattam was created in Kerala, India, under the patronage of Veera Kerala Varma (AD 1653–1694), known as Kottarakkara Thampuran.

Its creation was catalyzed by an insult from King Manavedan, the Zamorin of Kozhikode, who in 1657 AD refused to send his Krishnattam troupe to perform at a wedding in Kottarakkara, stating the court would not understand it.
Spurred by political and artistic rivalry, Kottarakkara Thampuran composed an eight-part dance drama based on the epic Ramayana in the Manipravalam literary style.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ramanattam is a sacred temple art presenting the narrative of the epic Ramayana.

Its eight daily plays depict key spiritual and dramatic chapters: Puthrakameshti, Seetha Swayamvaram, Vicchinnabhishekam, Kharavadham, Balivadham, Thoranayudham, Sethubandhanam, and Yudham, ending with Rama's crowning at Ayodhya.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historic figures associated with Ramanattam include Veera Kerala Varma (Kottarakkara Thampuran, AD 1653–1694), who authored the plays and founded the art form; King Manavedan (Zamorin of Kozhikode), whose refusal to share Krishnattam sparked its creation; and Kottayath Thampuran, who later adapted Ramanattam into Kathakali.
Ramanattam originated in Kottarakkara in southern Kerala and heavily influenced the development of Kathakali at the Mridangashaileshwari temple in Muzhakkunn, northern Kerala.

Derived as a direct response to Krishnattam (created by Zamorin Raja of Calicut in 1657 AD), Ramanattam served as the foundational parent tradition that evolved into Kathakali under the development of Kottayath Thampuran.
